 Accuracy of prediction markets disputed after midterm elections
 1 hour, 2 minutes ago 
 by 
 Stuart A. Thompson The New York Times
 -->
 -->
 -->
 -->
 Comments 
 A Kalshi ad encouraging pedestrians to dispose their cigarettes based on who they think will win the Alaska Senate race is pictured on Capitol Hill on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Washington.

 Heading into Election Day, Republicans appeared likely to hold on to South Carolina's Senate seat. Sen. Darline Graham was running to succeed her older brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, for a full term, and she had received President Donald Trump's endorsement.
 Prediction markets, like Polymarket and Kalshi, tended to agree. On the morning of Nov. 3, online bettors had given Graham a roughly 70% chance of winning the race, fueled by more than $27 million in betting activity.
 As results began to come in Tuesday evening, the odds of her winning on Polymarket and elsewhere rapidly inverted. The Democratic challenger, Annie Andrews, was swept into power as part of a national wave of Democratic support, winning by about 90,000 votes, or 4.4 percentage points, as of Thursday.
 Whether prediction markets can accurately anticipate election results has become a key question after the midterms. An analysis by The New York Times, using statistical methods, found that for most of the midterm race, prediction markets performed no better than election forecasts, which produce odds using polling and other indicators instead of betting activity. But as Election Day neared, prediction markets performed better as forecasts and polling became stale.
 The platforms have gone from an obscure form of online betting -- allowing people to place wagers on nearly anything, from sports to pop culture -- to an international fixation worth billions of dollars. They work by allowing anyone to bet on the outcome of pretty much any event, with the money that users spend translating into odds that something will happen.
 Polymarket and Kalshi spent the midterm season boasting about their superiority to polls and election forecasts, claiming that bettors can correctly predict the future when working in large enough numbers -- the wisdom of the crowd. They have said they are more reactive than polls, which query voters over several days and use that information to estimate how many votes each candidate will receive.
 They have also claimed to beat election forecasters, which produce odds showing whether a candidate will win by using a complex blend of polling data with economic metrics, historical trends, expert opinion and other indicators.
 Kalshi and Polymarket are now seeking to use the results from Election Day to prove that they offer public value as a reliable predictor.
 "Polymarket was right," the company crowed on social media Wednesday.
 "Over the last few months, the people showed up on Kalshi to tell the world what they were going to do," Tarek Mansour, the CEO of Kalshi, posted Wednesday. "Last night, the megaphone was passed to them."
 The Times found, however, that the odds produced by prediction markets over the past three months before the midterms were no more accurate than those from prominent election forecasts produced by data gatherers such as Nate Silver, who created Silver Bulletin, an election forecast and newsletter.
 While the odds on prediction markets became more accurate in the days before Election Day, earlier betting activity produced odds that were less confident about the winner than some forecasts and were frequently less accurate.
 In a statement, Kalshi said producing odds that were competitive with sophisticated election forecasts -- even months before Election Day -- was proof of their predictive power. They also pointed to odds that improved as the election neared. That is partly because election forecasts are highly reliant on polling, which becomes stale by Election Day, forecasters said.
 "The claim that we're making, very simply put, is just that the election markets we have on our platform are well calibrated, up to say three months out, even with low participation," said Nicole Kagan, the head of Kalshi Research, the prediction market's analysis division.
 Polymarket did not respond to a request for comment.
 Testing Accuracy
 The Times used several approaches to assess how the prediction markets performed. The main method, called the Brier score, measures a forecast's accuracy while also considering its confidence. Imagine that a prediction market gave one candidate a 90% chance of winning. If that candidate lost, the forecast made a major error and its final score should reflect the size of that miss. But if the candidate had only a 51% chance of winning, the error is more forgivable. Brier scores consider those factors.
 Overall, Polymarket and Kalshi led election forecasts at certain moments but spent most of the election trailing forecasters.
 At multiple points between August and November, prediction markets were less accurate than two election forecasts scored by the Times: Silver Bulletin and FiftyPlusOne. Those election forecasts tended to produce more reliable odds that better reflected the realities in the race, even months before results were known. When they favored the wrong candidate, they tended to assign lower odds than prediction markets, leaving open the possibility for an upset. When they chose the correct candidate, they were generally more confident.
 In Maine's Senate race, forecasters gave Troy Jackson, the Democrat, a better shot of defeating Susan Collins, the incumbent Republican, than prediction markets. That was true 30 days before the election and on Nov. 3, when prediction markets grew more confident about Jackson's odds but forecasters grew even more confident.
 Still, prediction markets generally fell in the middle of the accuracy rankings when compared with forecasts. That may be inevitable: Large groups of bettors combine information from all available sources, including election forecasts, into their decisions, creating what could amount to an average belief.
 "The markets are downstream of all those other signals," said Flip Pidot, chief business officer at High Roller Technologies, an online gambling and prediction markets company. "All the polls, all the forecasters, all the commentary, all the early-vote data, all the real-time data coming out -- that all gets fed into the market."
 That dynamic appeared to play out on election night, when prediction markets reacted to results in real time, producing highly confident predictions far before races were called by organizations such as The Associated Press. Almost as soon as polls closed, odds on prediction markets began shifting as early indications pointed to a tsunami of Democratic support.
 In Iowa's Senate race, polls were fairly evenly split between Josh Turek, the Democrat, and Ashley Hinson, the Republican. Thirty days before the election, forecasters gave the edge to Turek, while prediction markets favored Hinson.
 Turek ended up winning by more than 4 percentage points.
 Prediction markets may have slightly favored Republicans overall because of a false belief that polls always underestimate support for Republicans.
 The consensus after Election Day is that polls this year were, in general, on the mark. A New York Times/Siena poll, published Oct. 28, surprised pundits by showing that the Senate race in South Carolina had become a toss-up.
 "In general, prediction markets have done better than the polls in recent cycles because they've correctly anticipated the sign of a polling error," said Eric Zitzewitz, a Dartmouth University professor who has studied prediction markets. "It looks like, in this case, prediction markets were thinking there might be a slight overstatement of Democratic support in the polls -- and it looks like we sort of had the opposite."
